entries.clue: Underwear gaffes (8)

blocks.note: long, loose knickers of the Victorian kind
a bloomer is an embarrassing blunder

annotation.surface: A list of wardrobe malfunctions: someone's underwear is on show.
annotation.walkthrough: Two words, two meanings of one answer; 'bloomer' for a blunder is informal British usage.
annotation.definitionFit: Bloomers are old-fashioned baggy knickers, and bloomers are also howlers or gaffes.

entries.clue: Was Cameron covering up fraud? (4)

indicatorNotes.covering up: the phrase 'Was Cameron' covers the answer inside it

annotation.surface: A suspicious question about whether David Cameron, the former Prime Minister, was hiding a fraud.
annotation.walkthrough: The political scandal story is a smokescreen: the answer sits across the join of 'Was' and 'Cameron'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a con trick or swindle is both a fraud and, informally, a scam.

entries.clue: Likes playing with name in greeting capital (8)

indicatorNotes.playing: the letters of LIKES are played around with, rearranged
indicatorNotes.in: the rearranged letters go inside the greeting

blocks.note: hi = a greeting; it holds the rest

annotation.surface: Someone who enjoys toying with a name in a big-city welcome.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Likes' reads as a verb, but it is only letters to shuffle; 'greeting capital' sounds like a welcoming city, yet the greeting wraps round and 'capital' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Finland's seat of government is one capital among many.

entries.clue: Member, dithering Lib – ultimately Conservative, that's plain (7)

indicatorNotes.dithering: a dithering LIB can't keep its letters in order

blocks.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body

annotation.surface: A Liberal member of parliament wavers before finally siding with the Conservatives, and that much is obvious.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Member' in a political surface suggests an MP, but here it is a body part. 'Plain' means clear to read.
annotation.definitionFit: Legible writing is plain, clear enough to read.

entries.clue: Mars Bush's grasp of English? (6)

indicatorNotes.grasp of: the bush's grasp holds E inside it

blocks.note: a bush is a plant; it holds the next piece

annotation.surface: A dig at George W. Bush's famously shaky command of the English language, which 'mars' his speeches.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mars' looks like a verb (spoils) with Bush as its object; it is the noun, the red planet. 'Bush' is the shrub, not the president.
annotation.definitionFit: Mars is a planet, so it stands for the answer by example.

entries.clue: Bold creep abandons heroin chic (6)

indicatorNotes.abandons: INCH walks out of the phrase, leaving the rest

blocks.note: the phrase to be cut down
to creep = to inch along; these four letters go: HERO(INCH)IC

annotation.surface: Some unpleasant man turns his back on the gaunt, wasted fashion look of the 1990s.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heroin chic' was a 1990s fashion style of pale, emaciated models. 'Creep' reads as a nasty person but is the verb, giving INCH.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a daring, fearless act can be called bold or heroic.

entries.clue: "Badenoch's main deficiency": magazine reveals result of fight? (5,3)

indicatorNotes.main: the main, leading letter of Badenoch

blocks.note: Private Eye, the magazine this puzzle appears in

annotation.surface: A satirical magazine exposes a failing of Kemi Badenoch, leader of the UK Conservative Party.
annotation.walkthrough: The quoted headline suggests a political exposé; 'magazine' is Private Eye itself, the British satirical magazine that prints this crossword.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: a punch to the face in a brawl leaves bruising round the socket.

entries.clue: Act shocked about catching church sexual predator (6)

blocks.note: to reel = to stagger back in shock

annotation.surface: Someone feigns outrage at a church harbouring a sex offender.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Act shocked' is a full verb phrase for one word: to stagger back in surprise. The 'act' is not pretence.
annotation.definitionFit: A lecher is a lustful man who pursues women.

entries.clue: Clubs get irate about cancer risk (9)

indicatorNotes.about: the letters of GET IRATE are knocked about

annotation.surface: Golf or night clubs becoming angry about a health warning.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as 'concerning', but it tells you to rearrange GET IRATE.
annotation.definitionFit: Smoking cigarettes is a leading cause of cancer, so a cigarette is a cancer risk.

entries.clue: Conservative member initially falling into disregard gets percentage (10)

indicatorNotes.falling into: something that falls into a hole ends up inside it, so M drops inside OMISSION

blocks.note: an omission = a thing disregarded or left out; it takes in the next piece
first letter of member, placed after the O: O(M)MISSION

annotation.surface: A Conservative MP who first slips into ignoring the rules ends up taking a cut.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a sleaze story; commission is the percentage paid to an agent or broker.
annotation.definitionFit: A commission is a fee calculated as a percentage of a sale.

entries.clue: Idiot fellow in pursuit of muck (4)

blocks.note: F = fellow; it comes after, in pursuit of, GOO

annotation.surface: A foolish man chasing after filth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In pursuit of' is a position instruction: F follows GOO.
annotation.definitionFit: A goof is a silly, foolish person.

entries.clue: Old band crew's lackey (3-3)

blocks.note: to crew a ship = to man it

annotation.surface: A roadie who fetches and carries for an ageing rock group.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crew' looks like a noun (the band's road crew) but is the verb, meaning to man.
annotation.definitionFit: A yes-man agrees with everything the boss says, like a servile lackey.

entries.clue: Pissed over lower regions (played for maximum disturbance) (5,4)

annotation.definitionNote: the answer is the noun phrase in the idiom 'play merry hell'; the clue gives the whole idiom

blocks.note: pissed = drunk in British slang; merry = tipsy

annotation.surface: A drunk sprawled across someone's nether parts.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts MERRY above HELL. 'Pissed' is British slang for drunk, not angry.
annotation.definitionFit: To play merry hell is to cause as much trouble and disruption as possible.

entries.clue: Turned on by the ultimately risqué state of being educated (8)

blocks.note: a lamp turned on is lit

annotation.surface: Someone aroused by something naughty, dressed up as a lesson.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned on' reads as aroused, which fits 'risqué', but it means switched on: LIT.
annotation.definitionFit: Literacy is the state of being able to read and write, of being educated.

entries.clue: Sleazy way one's grabbed by bastard (6)

indicatorNotes.grabbed by: SOD grabs the other pieces and holds them

blocks.note: sod = an unpleasant person, British slang; it holds the rest
I = one, the Roman numeral; RD and I sit together inside SOD

annotation.surface: A seedy scene of someone being grabbed by a nasty man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sod' is a mild British insult, much like bastard.
annotation.definitionFit: Sordid means sleazy, dishonourable, grubby.

entries.clue: Hold your tongue in prison? (4,2)

annotation.surface: Advice to stay silent while behind bars.
annotation.walkthrough: The same phrase is a command to be quiet and a description of someone locked up.
annotation.definitionFit: Shut up means be quiet, and a prisoner is shut up in a cell.

entries.clue: Got an erection by chance? That's inopportune (4,4)

blocks.note: vulgar: to have got an erection is to be hard

annotation.surface: An untimely erection, and a sympathetic 'bad timing'.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By chance' looks like one phrase meaning accidentally; split it, and 'by' simply means next to.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Hard luck!' is what you say when something has happened unfortunately.

entries.clue: I'd missed, say, Putin's awards (8)

indicatorNotes.missed: the letters of I'D go missing

blocks.note: Putin is, for example, a president; with the 's that is PRESIDENTS

annotation.surface: Someone confesses they overlooked the medals and honours handed out by Putin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks Putin as an example of a president; the possessive 's supplies the final S.
annotation.definitionFit: Presents are gifts, and 'presents' also means gives or awards.

entries.clue: Very attractive sort of headbanger? (7)

blocks.note: one who stuns, as by a bang on the head

annotation.surface: Asking whether a gorgeous person might be a heavy-metal fan.
annotation.walkthrough: A headbanger is really a head-shaking metal fan; the question mark flags the literal reading, someone who bangs heads and so stuns.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: informally, someone so good-looking they leave you dazed; literally, anything that knocks you senseless with a blow to the head.

entries.clue: Barely performing, young Jack, initially (swamped by desire) (4,4)

blocks.note: lust = desire; it holds the next piece
first letters of Young Jack: L(YJ)UST

annotation.walkthrough: 'Barely performing' reads as one phrase; the definition is only 'Barely', and 'performing' gives ON.
annotation.definitionFit: Only just means barely, by the narrowest margin.

entries.clue: Mathematician went on screwing (6)

indicatorNotes.screwing: WENT ON is screwed up, twisted into a new order

annotation.surface: A mathematician who carried on having sex.
annotation.walkthrough: The saucy surface hides a plain rearrangement of WENT ON.

entries.clue: Sun restrained? Just a bit, so protest! (6)

indicatorNotes.Just a bit: only a bit of 'Sun restrained' is wanted

annotation.surface: A joke about the Sun newspaper being only mildly muzzled, followed by a call to protest.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper; that reading is a decoy for a run of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: street demonstrations and strikes are both protest and civil disorder of this kind.

entries.clue: Ever prepared before last two instalments of Yes Minister? (6)

indicatorNotes.prepared: EVER is prepared, made into a new form

entries.clue: Start to take piss – "cutesy!" (4)

annotation.walkthrough: 'Take the piss' is British slang for mock, but here 'piss' is literal: WEE.

entries.clue: Chief troublemaker puts halo on Trump? (10)

entries.clue: Clot dumps wife for colleague (4)

indicatorNotes.dumps: the clot dumps W and loses it

blocks.note: a wally is a fool, British slang

entries.clue: Lots of twits wanting tip from Elon (6)

entries.clue: Key agency head dead – refer to a higher-up (8)

blocks.note: the Escape key on a keyboard
